mo_d_vineyard.blurb: Vineyard is a long, scoop-shaped wall in the south section of Robinson Bluff, a bolted bluff above the Big River in eastern Missouri. It holds ten sport routes, running from easy 5.7 up through a handful of 5.10s with a single 5.11, so it suits a mixed group better than a hardcore project wall. Lines are tall, roughly 50 to 110 feet, and the style swings from steep slab to vertical. The wall sits in shade through summer afternoons and picks up sun on winter mornings, which stretches the useful season. It was once smothered in vines, and the base is reached by following the bluff trail south past the neighbouring Legacy Wall.

mo_slabtown.blurb: Slabtown is a small section of the Trapper's Camp riverside bluffs near Osceola, on the Truman Lake shore in west-central Missouri. It is the first stretch of cliff south of the main trail down from the road. Ten routes, six bolted and four traditional, run mostly from 5.8 to 5.10, with one easier line at 5.7 and a single 5.11 at the top end. The limestone is slabby to vertical and is described as fairly good here. Bring a standard sport rack plus some gear, and check lake levels beforehand since high water can flood the bases along this bluff.

mo_2_undercut_area.blurb: Undercut Area is the second sector along the Monegaw Springs sandstone crag in west-central Missouri, just past the Burns Side wall. A roof of about seven feet runs along the path at the base, with mostly vertical climbing on the face above it. All ten routes are bolted sport lines, concentrated in the 5.10 and 5.11 range with a couple of harder 5.12 and 5.13 lines at the top end. The crag as a whole faces south, though the base of the climbs usually has some shade. It is a short walk of a few minutes from the dirt parking area, making it a convenient day-trip stop for steady-grade sport climbers.

mo_3_the_refuge.blurb: The Refuge is the far end of the Monegaw Springs sandstone crag in west-central Missouri, reached by continuing along the base past the Burns Side and Undercut sectors. Overhangs of 10 to 20 feet cap the wall, and it is regarded as one of the state's best spots for roof climbing. Ten lines are here: mostly bolted sport routes, with one traditional line and a hard boulder problem. Grades start around 5.11 and climb well into 5.12 and 5.13, so this is a section for strong climbers rather than beginners. The crag overall faces south, but the base of the climbs often keeps some shade.
